article_title: Nature, Nurture, and the Meaning of Educational Attainment: Differences by Sex and Socioeconomic Status.
citation: Arpawong, Thalida Em; Gatz, Margaret; Zavala, Catalina; Gruenewald, Tara L.; Walters, Ellen E.; Prescott, Carol A. (2023). Nature, Nurture, and the Meaning of Educational Attainment: Differences by Sex and Socioeconomic Status. Twin Research and Human Genetics. https://doi.org/10.1017/thg.2023.6
title: Gene-by-environment opportunity-structure account of educational attainment
description: The article advances an explanatory account in which nurture moderates nature: "critical interrelationships exist, with nurture moderating effects of nature to alter the range of influence possible on EA". Genetic propensity for EA is expressed to different degrees depending on rearing household economic resources and on sex-linked social experiences, so EA "does not mean the same thing across people". In this early-1940s U.S. cohort, men could pursue genetically driven talents across socioeconomic strata, while women could do so only in the highest HES group, and the middle stratum for women showed the largest genetic constraint with outsized shared-family influence.
requirements: Requires a genetically informative design (twin and sibling data) to decompose genetic, shared, and unique environmental variance components.
Requires a direct, prospectively measured indicator of rearing socioeconomic context rather than retrospective or proxy measures.
constraints: The authors state results are likely cohort-specific to individuals born between 1940 and 1961 and that causal associations cannot be concluded.
Limited power to test effects of other social constraints, such as racial/ethnic inequalities, and siblings included were all siblings of twins.
target_learners: adolescents in U.S. high schools (cohort born early 1940s)
target_learning_goals: understanding how genetic and environmental influences on educational attainment differ by sex and rearing socioeconomic context
examples: The article notes that "null results in phenotypic models that test sex interactions do not preclude there being differences in etiologies for men and women," motivating biometric moderation modeling.
